chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Mahziyar who said:

'Isa ibn Ja'far ibn 'Isa asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) the second: 'A woman breast-fed a child for me, so is it permissible for me to marry the daughter of her husband?' He (peace be upon him) said to me: 'How excellent is what you asked from here; it may be that the people will say,

So I said to him (peace be upon him): 'The girl is not the daughter of the woman who breast-fed for me, she is the daughter of someone else.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Even if there were ten [women] scattered [in different places], nothing would be permissible for you from them, and they would be in the place of your daughters.'

key_terms.لَبَنِ الْفَحْلِ: Milk of the stallion (father), referring to the attribution of milk to the male head of the household
key_terms.مَوْضِعِ بَنَاتِكَ: In the place/position of your daughters
key_terms.مُتَفَرِّقَاتٍ: Scattered/different (referring to women in different locations)

ai.seo_question: Does a woman's husband's daughter become my milk-sister if she breastfed me?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* elucidates the principle of *rad al-rahib* (m of the stallion), where a man’s milk is attributed to his wife, thereby extending the prohibition of marriage to her daughters from other marriages. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that the husband's milk acts as a unifying agent, making his female offspring from any wife his milk-sisters, a ruling derived from the Quranic verse on breastfeeding. This establishes a robust framework for *mahram* relationships in Shia jurisprudence, emphasizing the social and familial bonds created through nursing.
